Keppel Reit to acquire 51% stake in Keppel South Central valued at $626.2 mil
article:
Keppel is selling a 51% interest in Keppel South Central to Keppel Reit. In an Oct 20 bourse filing, the Reit’s manager said it has entered into a conditional share purchase agreement to acquire the interest from its sponsor at an agreed property value of $626.2 million, or $2,350 psf.

The purchase consideration for the 51% interest is estimated at around $610.9 million, excluding goods and services tax.

While Keppel South Central is a freehold asset, Keppel Reit is acquiring the stake on a 70-year leasehold basis. After that period, the Reit will enter into an option deed granting Keppel the right to buy back the stake.

Keppel South Central is a 33-storey commercial building at 10 Hoe Chiang Road that was completed early last year. The freehold development has a gross floor area of 549,793 sq ft, and a net lettable area of approximately 522,500 sq ft. It has an occupancy rate of 52.7%, based on committed leases and leases in the process of documentation as of Sept 30.

As part of the acquisition, Keppel will provide Keppel Reit a guaranteed monthly income of $2.23 million for up to five years. The arrangement offers income stability while allowing Keppel REIT to "participate in potential future upside from the continued lease-up of the property", the Reit’s manager said.

Taking this into account, the acquisition translates to an initial property yield of 4.3%.

The deal also offers a pro forma distribution per unit (DPU) accretion of 2.01%. This assumes the acquisition, along with Keppel Reit's earlier announced divestments of Seoul office T Tower and Tokyo office KR Ginza II, had been completed on Jan 1, 2025.

The proposed income support arrangement is backed by rents at Keppel South Central, which currently average around $11.30 psf per month (psf pm) based on committed leases and leases in the process of documentation as of Sept 30.

The figure is higher than the $11.15 psf pm assumed under the arrangement, said the manager. In addition, the average rent largely reflects leasing activity on the lower-to-mid-floors, while remaining space on the higher floors could potentially command higher rents.

The manager added that as of Oct 15, committed leases and leases in the process of documentation had increased to about 60%.

Keppel Reit’s purchase of the 51% stake will be financed through a combination of bank loans, perpetual securities and equity financing.

The transaction is subject to approval of Keppel Reit’s unitholders at an extraordinary general meeting expected to be held in 4Q2026. The deal is targeted for completion in 2Q2027.

The acquisition will increase Keppel Reit’s Singapore presence to 82%, reinforcing its position in the supply-constrained CBS office market, said Chua Hsien Yang, CEO of the Reit’s manager. “With an acquisition structure that provides income stability and potential future upside, the transaction positions us well to deliver sustainable long-term returns for our unitholders.”

On a pro forma basis, assuming the proposed acquisition of Keppel South Central and both the divestments of T Tower and KR Ginza II had been completed on June 30, Keppel Reit's portfolio occupancy would be 93.9% across 13 properties, with a weighted average lease expiry of 4.5 years.

title: Beyond Blue Chips: 3 SGX Dividend Stocks Offering 6%+ Yields
article:
Singapore’s stock market has lost some of its shine recently.
As at 16 October 2026, the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) sat more than 7% below its all-time high.
For income investors, a
market pullback
brings a familiar temptation.
As share prices fall, headline dividend yields naturally rise.
However, a
high yield
only pays off if the underlying business can actually sustain its payouts.
For each of the three stocks below, we’ll ask one question: what pays for the dividend?

Can Valuetronics afford to pay out more as profit falls?
Valuetronics is an electronics manufacturing services provider with factories in China and Vietnam.
For its financial year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026), revenue slipped 4.0% year on year (YoY) to HK$1.66 billion.
The Industrial and Commercial Electronics division expanded 6.2% to HK$1.45 billion, but Consumer Electronics revenue dropped 41.7% as management actively phased out low-margin legacy products.
Net profit took a bigger hit, falling 33.1% to HK$111.4 million.
This was primarily driven by a HK$48.4 million net loss tied to its Trio AI investment alongside a higher tax bill.
Strip out the Trio AI impact, and underlying net profit came in at HK$159.9 million.
So why did the dividend go up?
Valuetronics changed its policy.
It now aims to pay out 50% to 70% of net profit, up from 30% to 50%.
It also lifted its total dividend by 41% to HK$0.38 per share, including a HK$0.16 special dividend.
Cash flow backs this up.
Free cash flow swung to HK$178.4 million from negative HK$20.1 million a year earlier, as capital expenditure fell to HK$47 million from HK$228 million following heavy prior investments in GPUs and AI hardware.
Cash rose to HK$1.21 billion, and the company has no bank borrowings.
Management also plans to return about HK$300 million in surplus cash over FY2027 and FY2028 through special dividends and share buybacks.
On the flip side, a higher payout ratio means future dividends will move more closely with profit.
Management expects to stay profitable in FY2027, but it has flagged a fluid environment amid US tariffs and supply-chain uncertainty.
If you buy, value the stock on its ordinary payout, not the specials.

Beyond Blue Chips: 3 SGX Stocks Quietly Buying Back Their Own Shares
3 Small-Cap SGX Stocks to Fund Your Retirement
What keeps HRnetGroup’s dividend rising when hiring slows?
HRnetGroup is a pan-Asian recruitment and staffing firm, specialising in permanent placement and contract staffing.
Revenue for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) dipped 1.1% YoY to S$292.2 million, though it was flat on a constant-currency basis, while contractor headcount rose 6.9% to 17,253.
HRnet squeezed more profit out of its revenue.
Gross margin widened to 21.3% from 20.7%, and operating expenses fell 1.9%.
Operating profit rose 9.4% to S$20.1 million.
The picture gets weaker below the operating line.
Other income fell 65.5% to S$5.4 million on lower government subsidies, a fair-value loss on investments and reduced interest income.
The decline weighed on net profit.
Free cash flow fell to S$17.4 million from S$26.5 million a year earlier.
The good news is that HRnet has no bank borrowings.
As at 30 June 2026, it held S$332.1 million in cash, treasury bills and gold.
This strong capital cushion allowed management to raise the interim dividend by 10% to S$0.022 per share, even as listed peers reported losses and underwent restructuring.
Here’s the thing: HRnet’s balance sheet gives the dividend a cushion, but free cash flow shrank by about a third.
Management says the industry remains under cyclical pressure.
If you own it, watch whether cash flow recovers.
Related articles:
3 Cash-Rich SGX Dividend Stocks With Over 4% Yield
Beyond STI: 3 Singapore Dividend Stocks Offering Steady Passive Income
Is UHREIT’s 10.5% yield a bargain or a warning?
United Hampshire US REIT (UHREIT) owns 21 grocery-anchored and necessity-based retail properties in the US, plus two self-storage properties.
The portfolio is valued at US$798.5 million.
In 1H2026, net property income (NPI) grew 6.4% YoY to US$25.5 million, while total distributable income expanded 5.8% to US$13.7 million.
Distribution per unit (DPU) rose by a smaller 3.4% to US$0.0216.
Why the gap?
UHREIT issued new units under its distribution reinvestment plan and as payment of the manager’s performance fee, increasing the total unit count to 608.2 million from 596.9 million.
Occupancy held firm.
Committed occupancy at the grocery and necessity properties stood at 97.6%, and self-storage occupancy improved by 430 basis points to 93.5%.
Acquisitions helped too.
Dover Marketplace and Wallingford Fair made their first contributions.
UHREIT bought Wallingford Fair for US$21.4 million, 8.2% below its independent valuation.
So what’s behind a 10.5% yield?
A yield this high suggests the market has doubts.
For a REIT, those doubts often sit on the balance sheet.
The manager also did not disclose rental reversion.
Before you buy, check UHREIT’s gearing and interest coverage ratio.

title: Nscale, Anthropic in talks for US$45 bil cloud computing deal — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 20): Nscale Ltd, the artificial intelligence (AI) cloud computing firm, is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic PBC in a deal that could be worth about US$45 billion ($57.5 billion), according to people familiar with the negotiations.

The Nvidia Corp-backed data centre developer is seeking a second major deal with the firm behind Claude for a second facility at its Monarch data centre campus in West Virginia, the people said. Anthropic has agreements in place with Nscale for infrastructure that’s worth as much as about US$44.6 billion, according to a regulatory filing for Nscale’s planned initial public offering (IPO).

The second Monarch building would deliver 460 megawatts of computing power, using Nvidia’s advanced Vera Rubin AI chips, some of the people said. Anthropic also has the right of first refusal on Monarch’s expected third building, they said.

A deal could be finalised as soon as in the coming days, the people said, asking not to be identified as the discussions are private. Deliberations are ongoing, details of the plan could change and no final decisions have been made, the people said. Representatives of Anthropic and Nscale declined to comment.

Another multibillion-dollar computing deal would bolster Nscale’s IPO prospects as it seeks about a US$30 billion valuation in its market debut. A cohort of investors urged the firm to lower its IPO valuation target, Bloomberg News has reported.

Anthropic, which is one of Nscale’s biggest customers, has emerged as a major client for data centre providers in general. Deals it has inked include a US$50 billion pact with Fluidstack Ltd, US$10 billion with infrastructure start-up Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd and US$45 billion with Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

See also: AEM’s Kabbani stresses company’s tech chops to ride on AI-driven semi-con wave

Nscale’s Monarch campus in West Virginia is scalable to more than eight gigawatts of gross power when complete, the IPO filing documents showed.

Part of the Monarch campus was initially expected to be leased by Microsoft Corp, which had announced in March it signed a letter of intent for the planned data centre. But Microsoft walked away from the West Virginia site in the summer, allowing Anthropic to become the tenant, Bloomberg News reported.

Anthropic, which was valued at US$965 billion in May, is expected to conduct its own potentially record-breaking IPO in the coming months, and continues to hunt for more computing power to keep growing.

See also: The AI industry isn’t ready for the coming AI catastrophe

Investors have grown increasingly wary of the vast sums being borrowed to finance the AI data centre boom, souring on everything from chipmakers’ stocks to the debt of cloud-computing firms.

Nscale filed publicly for a US listing in September, and has yet to begin formal marketing even though the required 15 day waiting period has elapsed. The company is working through comments from the US Securities and Exchange Commission on its filing, and intends to kick off marketing when those are resolved, people familiar with the matter have said.

The company raised US$3.36 billion in a pre-IPO financing round last month in a deal led by Dan Loeb’s Third Point with investors including Nvidia, Apollo Global Management Inc, Citadel, Hudson Bay Capital and Abu Dhabi Investment Council participating.

title: Asian LNG prices jump to highest since 2022 on tanker strikes
article:
(Oct 20): Asian liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices rose to the highest in almost four years, as attacks on tankers in the Middle East damped hopes for a recovery in exports from the war-torn region.

Spot prices jumped to US$30.4 per million British thermal units on Monday, according to traders, the highest since December 2022. The UK Maritime Trade Operations received a report over the weekend that an LNG carrier was fired on near Yemen on Saturday, part of a recent increase in strikes on oil and gas vessels in the Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz.

The US-Iran war has trapped most Qatari LNG production, which used to account for about a fifth of global supply, behind Hormuz, forcing buyers to turn to the more expensive spot market as they can’t get enough contracted deliveries. That’s coinciding with an increase in demand as the Northern Hemisphere winter approaches, pushing prices to three times the level they were at before the conflict started in late February.

Some Asian buyers are continuing to buy spot shipments at the high price levels, intensifying competition for the super-chilled fuel with Europe. Gas-storage levels there are at 75% full, compared with a five-year seasonal average of 89%.

The energy crunch is boosting household power bills and inflation, while forcing some economies to rely more heavily on coal. South Korea’s energy minister said last week that the country would lean on the dirtiest fossil fuel and nuclear power to cope with a jump in electricity demand over winter.

See also: Qatar LNG cargo makes rare Red Sea journey to get gas to Europe

title: Takaichi reaffirms no deficit bonds to fund food sales tax cut
article:
(Oct 20): Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reiterated that she won’t rely on special deficit-covering bonds to fund a sales tax cut on food after her earlier remarks sparked speculation that she was changing her stance.

In a post on X late Monday, Takaichi wrote that she isn’t ruling out issuing government bonds to fund the national budget as a whole but she won’t rely on special deficit-covering bonds to cover a shortfall in income from the temporary sales tax cut.

The government’s position “remains unchanged,” she wrote. Takaichi said she was clarifying her position after some media reports appeared to misrepresent remarks she made earlier Monday in parliament.

At a budget committee meeting of the upper house, Takaichi said she wouldn’t rule out issuing government bonds when asked about how the sales tax cut would be funded.

“Regarding funding for the consumption tax rate reduction on food and beverages, within the broader framework of budget formulation reform, we will carefully examine the fiscal scale that would also enable us to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio while closely monitoring tax revenue trends and proceeding with a review of both expenditures and revenues,” Takaichi said.

“We will appropriately control the total annual issuance of government bonds through both the initial budget and supplementary budgets, just as we did last fiscal year. This does not mean we are ruling out the issuance of government bonds,” she said.

The market has been paying close attention to how Takaichi would fund the sales tax cut, which is expected to cost ¥5 trillion (US$31.5 billion) per year, without further straining the nation’s debt burden. The temporary tax cut is expected to start in April and last for two years.

title: Data centre firm Elice plunges 33% in debut sunk by AI worry
article:
(Oct 20): Data-centre infrastructure company Elice Inc plunged in its trading debut in South Korea, dragged down by swirling concern about the outlook for the industry.

Shares of the Seoul-based neocloud service provider fell as much as 33% to 61,000 won in early Tuesday trading on the tech-heavy Kosdaq market, on track for the worst-ever opening day after a sizable Korean initial public offering. The company raised 201 billion won (US$151 million) in the IPO, pricing its shares at 90,500 won apiece, the top of a marketed price range, for a post-listing market capitalisation exceeding one trillion won. The retail offering was subscribed more than 400 times.

The debut is a reflection of souring investor appetite for the sector after a series of setbacks around the world. Firmus Grid Ltd cancelled its high-profile Sydney listing this month as concerns over borrowing costs, fierce competition and long-term returns from massive AI-related spending weigh on valuations. Coreweave Inc’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, AirTrunk is delaying a planned IPO of a real estate investment trust, people familiar with the matter have said, while Nscale Ltd is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, Bloomberg News reported.

“Elice’s debut comes at a time when sentiment towards AI infrastructure companies has weakened, particularly in the US,” said Albert Yong, managing partner and chief investment officer at Petra Capital Management. “Sentiment towards AI infrastructure has been highly volatile and often disconnected from underlying fundamentals.”

In a sign of regulatory pushback in the broader industry, South Korea is examining whether a proposed US initial public offering of SK Hynix Inc’s unit Solidigm would count as a “duplicate listing,” as some lawmakers push for stronger protection of minority shareholders.

See also: Samsung, SK Hynix slide causes US$137 bil South Korean pension hit

Elice was able to generate demand among South Korean retail investors, who poured roughly 10.3 trillion won into subscription deposits in hopes of buying shares. But if the 33% drop holds, it would become the worst-ever debut after a Korea IPO that raised at least US$100 million, surpassing the 30% plunge by W-Scope Chungju Plant Co in 2022.

“The healthy retail order book for Elice’s listing is a testament to investors’ eagerness to participate in what will surely be a massive need for AI infrastructure in the coming years,” said Hans Stege, head of investment research at PrePublic Equity Partners. “But that buildout will require well-functioning debt markets as well, and we are seeing a lot of pencil sharpening around cash flows and capital stacks as a result.”

To win over investors, Elice touted a 200% surge in first-half revenue to 34.4 billion won, according to its prospectus. The company swung to an operating profit of 10.3 billion won, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation jumped more than 11-fold to 23.2 billion won. The company is expected to record an 83% sales jump in 2026 and an operating margin of about 33%, analyst Douglas Kim wrote in a note on Smartkarma.

See also: Meta says Claude AI tool triggered No Kings Instagram suspension

Elice’s financial structure is different from CoreWeave’s, and investors don’t need to view the company as “particularly risky,” said Kim Dojoon, chief executive officer at Zian Investment Management. But, he added, “It remains to be seen whether the company can maintain its current profitability.”

Founded in 2015 by three students in the doctorate programme of KAIST, one of the country’s top technology universities, Elice began as a coding education platform before pivoting to AI cloud infrastructure, supplying products including servers, liquid-cooled chips, cloud and networking equipment and software. The company has since developed a modular data centre platform with high-density power systems and advanced liquid cooling designed for high-performance AI chip clusters.

A successful offering could help break an IPO drought in South Korea, where the primary market has been in the doldrums as fundraising surged across Asia. First-time listings in Seoul have raised US$1.4 billion in 2026, compared with more than US$3 billion in each of the previous three years, according to Bloomberg-compiled data. Meanwhile, SK Hynix Inc completed the biggest-ever US share sale by a foreign company.

Elice’s IPO was the biggest on the Kosdaq this year and surpassed in Korea only by the US$337 million offering of K Bank Co in March.

Backed by venture capital firms including Vertex Ventures and Altos Ventures, Elice plans to use its IPO proceeds to build more AI data centres around South Korea and abroad, according to chief executive Officer Jae Won Kim. Mirae Asset Securities Co and Samsung Securities Co served as lead underwriters.

“We’re going all-in on becoming a full-stack AI infrastructure leader globally,” Kim said in an interview. “This IPO is about giving ourselves the financial firepower to execute.”

title: JPMorgan wealth advisers create firm overseeing US$18.6 bil
article:
(Oct 20): Two former JPMorgan Chase & Co wealth management partners have left the bank to launch their own firm managing US$18.6 billion in client assets, instantly making it one of the country’s biggest registered investment advisers.

Jim Atwood and Phil Scott announced Monday the creation of Latigo Peak Partners, a Palm Beach Gardens, Florida-based wealth advisory firm with 48 employees. The firm’s initial assets make it one of the largest “breakaway” deals in recent years, where advisers start a new firm and take many of their clients with them.

“There are not a lot of things out there where you get better as you get older. We’ve been doing this for 40 years, and plan on going for another 20 years,” Atwood said in an interview. “We want to build a family legacy business.”

Major employers have been taking notice of the trend: UBS Group AG recently increased compensation for thousands of its wealth advisers in the US after a series of high-profile exits from the firm. Last year, two other ex-JPMorgan bankers launched their own firm, Alta Vera Global Capital Advisors, managing US$400 million in assets.

Atwood, 65, and Scott, 71, both began their careers at Merrill Lynch and later joined First Republic, which was acquired by JPMorgan in 2023. They most recently worked alongside each other managing JPMorgan’s wealth units in Boston and Bellevue, Washington, respectively. That depth of experience helped convince them that starting their own firm would give them more flexibility in managing their clients’ assets.

See also: Morgan Stanley enters UK savings market with Raisin partnership

“If you’re working within one of these firms, you’re confined to investment opportunities on their platform,” Atwood said. “It gets difficult to be as nimble as you want.”

Latigo Peak will focus on public equity investing, and also offer a suite of services more typically associated with a multifamily office, including tax planning, estate planning and advice on philanthropic giving. The firm’s creation was first reported by Barron’s.

See also: PHP agrees £700 mil UK private hospital venture with GIC

The business is backed entirely by the partners’ own capital, bucking a yearslong trend of independent RIAs seeking outside financing to scale up their operations. Much of that money has come from PE: private equity backed 88% of all deals in the RIA industry last year, according to a Fidelity Investments report.

“If you look at at the top 25 RIAs, there are only one or two that are not PE-backed,” Atwood said. “We had a lot of opportunities out there to partner with PE — but when you partner with another firm, what comes with that is they’re going to want to get out in five or six years. They’re going to have an idea of how to manage the business.”

“Phil and I are backing this 100% ourselves, which is a big differentiator,” he added. “It’s not cheap to do that.”

Scott and Atwood said they generated combined revenue at JPMorgan of more than US$130 million, a nearly fourfold increase from six years prior. The plan is to keep growing: Atwood estimated that more than 95% of the firm’s new business is coming from word-of-mouth referrals.

Both Atwood and Scott have homes in the Palm Beach area, and chose the location for the firm’s headquarters in part because of the growing demand they saw for wealth management services in the region.

“A lot of people are starting to have liquidity events — there wasn’t nearly as much M&A activity five years ago as there is today,” Scott said.

Latigo Peak also has offices in Bellevue, Boston and Los Angeles, and is looking at opening locations in Denver and Jackson Hole, Wyoming, within a year, Scott said.

The firm is named in part for a ski run at the Beaver Creek resort in Colorado. Atwood and Scott met at the mountain 35 years ago, where they’ve long had an annual get-together with a number of industry colleagues.

“There’s a run out of Beaver Creek called Latigo. We used to put on the helmets and see who could get down the fastest,” Atwood said.
